A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is admitted to hospital with diabetic ketoacidosis.
She has no past medical history other than three episodes of retinal photocoagulation for diabetic retinopathy. She makes a good recovery.
Her blood tests show that she has mild renal impairment with a creatinine of 99 μ mol/L (eGFR 60 ml/min/1.73m). Her blood pressure is
116/43 mmHg. She has been adequately ﬂuid resuscitated and a renal ultrasound is unremarkable.
Her only medications are Lantus and NovoRapid insulins.
A random urine sample is sent to the laboratory for analysis. Microscopy is unremarkable and the urinary albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) isreported as 17 mg/mmol (<2.5).
What is the most appropriate course of action?
explanation:
This patient has type 1 diabetes with a history of related microvascular disease (diabetic retinopathy).
Microalbuminuria is deﬁned as an ACR of 2.5-30 mg/mmol in men and 3.5-30 mg/mmol in women. This is roughly equivalent to theloss of 30-300 mg of albumin in the urine per 24 hours.
In patients with diabetes, microalbuminuria is used as a therapeutic target that can be modiﬁed by renin-angiotensin-aldosteronesystem blockade with a resulting improvement in clinical outcomes.
All patients with diabetes and microalbuminuria should be offered therapy with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blockerirrespective of whether they have hypertension. The chosen drug should be started at an appropriate starting (low) dose and titratedupwards to the target dose as tolerated with monitoring of renal function.
The predominant protein lost in urine is albumin and the albumin:creatinine ratio is a signiﬁcantly more sensitive test for low levelproteinuria than the protein:creatinine ratio.

You admit a 48-year-old man who is on daily peritoneal dialysis in his own home. He noticed that his PD ﬂuid looked cloudier than usual thismorning.
Which of the following is most likely to be effective at treating the cause for his presentation?
explanation:
This patient had PD-related peritonitis, and the initial treatment of choice would be intraperitoneal antibiotics. These areadministered by adding them to the ﬂuid being instilled into the peritoneal cavity.
Typically a broad spectrum antibiotic cover is given pending PD ﬂuid culture results. Intravenous antibiotics would be preferable ifthe clinical condition worsened despite intraperitoneal antibiotics, or if there is an associated bacteraemia.
Removing the PD catheter should also be considered if the patient fails to settle.

explanation:
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines on the identiﬁcation and management of chronic kidney diseaserecommend that screening for chronic kidney disease should be offered to patients with:DiabetesHypertensionCardiovascular diseaseStructural renal tract pathologyMultisystem disease with potential renal involvementOpportunistically detected haematuria or proteinuriaA family history of stage 5 chronic kidney disease, orHereditary kidney disease.
In the absence of other risk factors the guidelines recommend that age, gender and ethnicity should not be used as risk markers totest people for chronic kidney disease.

explanation:
This patient most likely has paracetamol nephrotoxicity.
This can develop later than liver toxicity, and usually the renal function returns to baseline after a few weeks. Haemodialysis may berequired to support the patient during the acute episode.
Renal dysfunction in paracetamol overdose appears to occur in a dose-dependent manner; it is seen in only a small minority of allpatients, but up to half of those develop fulminant liver failure.
The mechanism of kidney injury is similar to that of the liver, but there is little evidence that N-acetyl cysteine confers any renalprotection.

A 40-year-old male is followed up in the renal clinic.
His creatinine clearance (measured) is 76 ml/min. A recent USS of his renal tract shows enlarged kidneys bilaterally, with multiple renal cysts.His father required dialysis at the age of 45 years.
On examination, his blood pressure is 149/88 mmHg.
Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: An ACE inhibitor would be appropriate to control his hypertension
Ciproﬂoxacin should be prescribed for upper urinary tract infections
He should be informed of the probable need for dialysis in ﬁve years
He should have follow up in renal clinic every 6 months
explanation:
This patient has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).
On average, patients progress to end stage renal failure between the ages of 40 and 60 years.
In these patients the renal function usually deteriorates in a gradual fashion, usually with a drop in creatinine clearance of 5/6ml/min/year (at least 10 years for this patient or possibly sooner if BP not adequately managed).
Treatment should include a high ﬂuid intake (to prevent the formation of renal stones or blood clots) and regular follow up of bloodpressure and renal function. Loin pain should be treated symptomatically, and hypertension should be managed with standardantihypertensive medications.
Haematuria should be treated conservatively. Urinary tract infections should be treated with lipophillic drugs (for example,ciproﬂoxacin, trimethoprim-sulphamethoxazole) as they have the best penetration into cyst ﬂuid.
It is an autosomal dominant disease, therefore the offspring of an affected patient has a 50% chance of inheriting the disease. Thepatient should be offered genetic counselling, despite the fact that the disease has a variable clinical course even between affectedfamily members.

A 60-year-old male patient presents to the Emergency department generally unwell.
You note that on his list of medications is acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. An arterial blood gas is taken.
What acid/base abnormality does acetazolamide have the potential of causing?
options: Metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap
Metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap
explanation:
Carbonic anhydrase catalyses the ﬁrst part of the reversible reaction in which carbon dioxide and water are converted to carbonicacid (and vice versa):
CO + HO ←→  H + HCO
In the kidney, carbonic anhydrase is found in the proximal convoluted tubule.
The equation is normally shifted to the left allowing the formed carbon dioxide to diffuse back into the systemic circulation. In thepresence of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, such as acetazolamide, the equation is shifted to the right and more H and HCO isproduced. The H is reabsorbed alongside chloride ions. However, the bicarbonate is passed in the urine as it is not easily absorbed
in the nephron. This results in a hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

A 68-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with transient dysphasia and left sided weakness affecting her face and arm.
Her past medical history is signiﬁcant for ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, and end-stage renal failure. She has haemodialysis everyMonday, Wednesday and Friday mornings.
A plain CT scan of the brain is reported as showing no evidence of an acute infarction or haemorrhage.
Your consultant decides to request further brain imaging, and asks you to liaise with the radiology department.
Which of the following statements applies to this patient?
options: She should not receive gadolinium-based contrast
She should not receive iodine-based contrast
She should not receive any form of contrast
She will need pre-hydration before she receives any contrast
explanation:
In patients with end-stage renal failure the use of gadolinium has been associated with nephrogenic systemic ﬁbrosis, and it shouldtherefore be avoided.
Renal failure is not in itself a contraindication to MRI scanning.
When patients are dialysis-dependent it would be potentially dangerous to "pre-hydrate" the patient and potentially ﬂuid overloadthem. Dialysis-dependent patients who receive contrast for a CT scan may need haemodialysis to remove the contrast. This isparticularly important when they have some residual renal function that should be preserved as far as possible (as it makes their ﬂuidbalance much easier to manage between dialysis sessions).
MR contrast tends not to be nephrotoxic and therefore haemodialysis is not usually necessary to remove MR contrast.

A 20-year-old male is referred to renal outpatients by his general practitioner.
He attends with his mother who explains that his father, from whom she has now separated, has recently been diagnosed with polycystickidney disease and has needed to start haemodialysis. His paternal aunt has kidney disease and suffered a subarachnoid haemorrhage dueto an intracranial aneurysm and his paternal grandfather died of 'kidney problems' aged 64.
His blood pressure is 129/64 mmHg, physical examination is unremarkable. His blood tests and urine dip are unremarkable. They wonderabout the possibility of screening for polycystic kidney disease.
If desired, which of the following tests is it most appropriate to offer the patient?
explanation:
The family history is indicative of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
Renal ultrasound screening is the test of choice and has 100% sensitivity for PKD1, false negatives may occur below the age of 20.
If cysts are not seen the ultrasound should be repeated every ﬁve years until the age of 30. Some authorities advocate commencingscreening at an earlier age (as young as seven to 10 years), this is because early diagnosis and management of hypertension canslow disease progression.
Abdominal CT is sensitive for the detection of cysts however the high radiation dose, particularly in young patients, means it is notwidely used as a screening test.
Genetic testing in the setting of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is only used in very particular circumstances - usuallyonly when a deﬁnite diagnosis is required in a young patient (for example, potential living donor). This is because sequence analysiscan identify only around 70% of known mutations and linkage analysis requires the availability of suﬃcient family members.
The use of intravenous urography in the diagnosis of polycystic kidney disease is purely historical.

explanation:
The ﬁndings are typical of a drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis.
Acute interstitial nephritis is characterised by interstitial inﬂammation and oedema. Left untreated this results in interstitial ﬁbrosis.A deﬁnitive diagnosis is established by renal biopsy, although eosinophiluria and gallium 67 scanning are also suggestive.
60-70% of cases of acute interstitial nephritis are induced by exposure to drugs. The mechanism is via a delayed T-cellhypersensitivity or cytotoxic T-cell reaction. This is not typically dose-dependent. Multiple medications have been implicated, andthe presentation and laboratory ﬁndings vary according to the class of drug involved.
Agents which are commonly implicated are:beta-lactam antibiotics (especially methicillin)sulphonamidesNSAIDsdiuretics (thiazides, furosemide)antivirals (aciclovir, foscarnet)allopurinol, andcyclosporin.
Classic presenting features include fever, maculopapular rash and arthralgia. Mild eosinophilia is common, and eosinophiuria ispathognomonic.

A 78-year-old man with diabetes had been on regular haemodialysis (four hours three times a week) for twelve years.
He presented complaining of increasing muscular aches, numbness and joint stiffness affecting his hands, arms and shoulders. His lowerlimbs were not affected. His medications include calcium carbonate two tablets three times a day with meals, ACE inhibitor, aspirin and 1-alpha calcidol 1 mcg once a day.

explanation:
All the above options can cause neurological abnormalities in patients with renal failure.
Aluminium toxicity can cause twitching, myoclonic jerks, motor apraxia, ﬁts and personality changes. It is now rare, due to treatmentof dialysis water with reverse osmosis, to remove the aluminium, and the use of calcium containing phosphate binders, instead ofaluminium.
Amyloidosis is a common cause of neurological impairment in patients on longstanding dialysis. It is caused by β 2 microglobulinaccumulation. It causes joint pains and stiffness, usually upper limbs more than lower limbs. The only treatment is renaltransplantation. It can be reduced by using high ﬂux dialysis membranes in patients who are likely to be on dialysis for a prolongedperiod.
The above symptoms do not ﬁt with cerebrovascular disease, as the symptoms spare the lower limbs.
Diabetic neuropathy again does not ﬁt with the above picture of symptoms sparing the lower limbs.
Uraemia may cause neurological symptoms. This is more common in men, and mostly affects the legs. Sensory symptoms(paraesthesia, burning sensations and pain) occur before motor symptoms (muscle atrophy, myoclonus, paralysis). The sensorysymptoms may improve with starting or increasing the frequency of dialysis, but the motor symptoms are not reversible.

A male patient with a background of sensorineural deafness is referred to the nephrology clinic due to microscopic haematuria and poorrenal function. He has a family history of kidney disease and a diagnosis of Alport syndrome is made.
His partner has just given birth to a boy.
Assuming the most common mode of inheritance of this condition, what is the likelihood of his son having the disease?
explanation:
Alport syndrome is caused by defects in the synthesis of type IV collagen. Type IV collagen is found in the basement membrane ofthe kidney, inner ear and eye, so therefore extra-renal manifestations include bilateral sensorineural deafness and ocularabnormalities such as corneal dystrophies and lens abnormalities.
Renal manifestations include microscopic and macroscopic haematuria with or without proteinuria, and eventual progression torenal failure.
The disease is X linked in 85% of cases because the most common genetic abnormality is a mutation in the COL4A5 gene (involvedin type IV collagen synthesis) on the X chromosome. COL4A3 and COL4A4 (genes also involved in type IV collagen synthesis) arelocated on chromosome 2, explaining why this disease may also have autosomal recessive or dominant inheritance.
Patients with Alport syndrome are at risk of developing antiglomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture's disease)following transplantation, as their immune systems have never been exposed to type IV collagen and hence lack tolerance.
Alport syndrome can be autosomal dominant, recessive or a new spontaneous mutation. However in 85% of cases it is X linked.Therefore, as only the Y chromosome is passed from father to son there is no chance of the son having the disease.

You are seeing a 34-year-old woman as a new patient in the renal clinic.
She recently had a renal tract ultrasound scan that was consistent with adult polycystic kidney disease. She tells you her mother and olderbrother have polycystic kidneys, and she is concerned that her 10-year-old son may have the diagnosis too.
She has no other past medical history and takes no regular medication. On examination in the clinic her blood pressure is 160/89 mmHg andurinalysis is negative.

options: Organise abdominal ultrasound scan for her son

explanation:
Patients with adult polycystic kidney disease (APKD) need strict blood pressure control in order to preserve renal function as long aspossible. This lady is hypertensive and accordingly she needs antihypertensive medication.
Her son is at risk of having APKD (autosomal dominant inheritance) but screening is not recommended until adulthood. He shouldhowever have his blood pressure monitored annually, and if he becomes hypertensive this should be aggressively managed. This isthe case whether or not ultrasound imaging reveals cysts in his kidneys. Formal urine protein quantiﬁcation would not add anythingwith a negative urinalysis.
Associated features of APKD include berry aneurysms, cysts in other organs (liver, pancreas, ovaries) and hypertension.
Screening for aneurysms is routinely considered only in patients with a personal or family history of intracranial haemorrhage.
The cysts in other organs are usually inconsequential and therefore checking the liver function tests is unhelpful in this context.

Contact surgical team immediately for removal of peritoneal dialysis catheter

explanation: In patients with chronic kidney disease maintaining the haemoglobin level within the normal range is associated with adverseoutcomes. A 19-year-old man presents with macroscopic haematuria that has been present for the last three days. He reports having a sore throat forthe last week.
On further questioning he reveals that a similar episode occurred two years ago but spontaneously resolved. His dipstick is positive for bloodand protein. Urine microscopy demonstrates red cell casts.
Blood tests reveal:
Sodium136 mmol/L(137-144)
Potassium4.8 mmol/L(3.5-4.9)
Urea 9.2 mmol/L(2.5-7.5)
Creatinine170 μ mol/L(60-110)
What is the most likely ﬁnding on renal biopsy?
options: Diffuse thickening of the basement membrane
explanation:
The case described is a classical presentation of IgA nephropathy, also known as IgA nephritis or Berger's disease.
The term synpharyngitic nephritis is sometimes used referring to the onset of haematuria and sore throat virtually simultaneously asin this case.
In post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis the onset of renal disease is usually some time (weeks) after the upper respiratory illness.
Mesangial widening, inﬂammation and mesangial cell proliferation are common features on renal biopsy in IgA nephropathy.Granular IgA deposits on immunoﬂuorescence are the hallmark of the disease and give it its name.

A 68-year-old man with IgA nephropathy is evaluated in the renal dialysis clinic for the ﬁrst time.
He is approaching stage 4 kidney disease and his renal physician is preparing him for dialysis in the near future. He is unable to undergoperitoneal dialysis due to a previous history of multiple abdominal surgeries.
Which of the answers below is the recommended ﬁrst choice for vascular access for routine haemodialysis?
explanation:
Current Renal Association guidelines state that an arterio-venous ﬁstula is the ﬁrst choice of vascular access for dialysis.
Planning for vascular access in patients with stage 4 kidney disease is essential to avoid the need for emergency dialysis.
Although there are a variety of options for vascular access, arterio-venous ﬁstulas are preferred due to their longevity and lower riskof infection.
Arterio-venous grafts, using prosthetic material, have a reduced longevity compared to arterio-venous ﬁstulas. These are secondchoice preference for vascular access.
Dialysis catheters, tunnelled and non-tunnelled carry a risk of infection and are not preferred as ﬁrst line. They can be used whenemergency dialysis is required, or as an interim measure when awaiting more permanent dialysis access.
A Hickman line is a permanent single lumen line inserted into the subclavian vein. It is often used to deliver antibiotics orchemotherapeutic agents but is not used for dialysis.
Reference:
The Renal Association. Vascular Access for Haemodialysis.

A 26-year-old female who is 13 weeks pregnant is seen in the outpatient clinic and noted to have a sustained blood pressure of 170/92mmHg. She has no past medical history of note and has otherwise been well and asymptomatic. This is her ﬁrst pregnancy.
Examination is otherwise generally normal and no abnormalities are noted on fundoscopy. Ultrasound examination of the kidneys showedboth kidneys to be of equal size of 9-10 cm. Urinalysis reveals protein (+) and blood (+).
What is the most likely cause of her hypertension?
explanation:
At 13 weeks of pregnancy, it is too early to present with pre-eclampsia.
Fibromuscular dysplasia does not typically present with dipstick haematuria.
Membranous GN is associated with a nephrotic syndrome and therefore one would expect more proteinuria and no haematuria.
This patient has normal sized kidneys, which would be unusual for reﬂux nephropathy.
IgA nephropathy can present with all the above features.

You are called to a normally ﬁt and well 65-year-old patient on the medical assessment unit. He was admitted earlier in the day withpneumonia and fulﬁlled the criteria for severe sepsis.
Despite adequate ﬂuid replacement over the course of the day his creatinine is 1200 μ mol/L and his urea is 30 mmol/L.
Which of the following would be the most appropriate reason for initiating renal replacement therapy in this patient?
options: Potassium of 5.0 mmmo/L after optimal medical therapy
Drop in haemoglobin from 100 g/L to 74 g/L
explanation:
The initiation of emergency renal replacement therapy is usually required for:Acute life threatening hyperkalaemia which is resistant to treatment. In this example the potassium is within normal limits.Development of metabolic acidosis which is non-responsive to ﬂuid. In this instance the pH is within normal limits.Development of ﬂuid overload, which may manifest itself as pulmonary oedema.Development of uraemia which may manifest itself as pericarditis (not pancreatitis), neuropathy and confusional state.
A drop in haemoglobin is not an indication for emergency renal replacement therapy. In this instance it maybe dilutional but sourcesof bleeding should be sought.
In chronic renal failure anaemia may result from a lack of erythropoietin production which can be treated with syntheticerythropoietin and iron infusion (not renal replacement therapy).
Reference:
UpToDate. Renal replacement therapy (dialysis) in acute kidney injury (acute renal failure) in adults: Indications, timing, and dialysisdose.

A 60-year-old woman presents with a three day history of nausea.
She takes no medication and the only relevant past medical history is diet controlled diabetes mellitus. At her most recent check there wasno clinical evidence of retinopathy or of neuropathy, and her creatinine was 79 µmol/L.
On admission to hospital her bloods show:
Na 139 mmol/L(137-144)
K 5.3 mmol/L(3.5-4.9)
Urea 35.5 mmol/L(2.5-7.5)
Creatinine895 μ mol/L(60-110)
Hb 91 g/L (115-165)
Which of the following is most likely to be positive?
explanation:
From the above options this patient with an acute kidney injury and anaemia is most likely to have anti-glomerular basementmembrane disease, otherwise known as Goodpasture's syndrome.
The background of diabetes mellitus is a red-herring, and serves only to tell you that her renal function was recently normal.
Patients presenting acutely with Goodpasture's tend to give a short history and can be systemically relatively well, besides symptomsof uraemia (nausea) and haematuria and/or haemoptysis.
ANCA-associated vasculitis can present in a similar fashion but the history is usually longer and the patient is systemically unwell atthe time of presentation.

A 24-year-old man with chronic renal failure underwent renal transplantation with a matched related donor graft.
The immediate post-operative period was uneventful and he was discharged home after two weeks with a fully-functioning graft. One monthlater he presented to the nephrology clinic with a high fever and he was admitted for further investigations.
His full blood count showed a marked leukopenia. During the ﬁrst evening of his admission, his clinical condition deteriorated rapidly and hebecame dyspnoeic. On reviewing the other investigations, his liver function tests were noted to be markedly deranged.
Which of the following is the most likely cause of his illness?
explanation:
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is responsible for a substantial fraction of the morbidity and mortality following organtransplantation.
Two main factors determine whether a patient will develop CMV infection after transplantation :1. Whether the donor or recipient harbours a latent virus capable of reactivation after transplantation2. The degree of immunosuppression after transplantation.
Primary disease is the commonest and most severe type of post-transplant CMV infection. This occurs in individuals who have neverbeen infected with CMV who receive an allograft that contains latent virus from a CMV-seropositive donor.

You are asked to prescribe synthetic erythropoietin to a patient on the general medical ward.
Which of the following is a relative contraindication?
explanation:
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents act as a growth factor in the context of active malignancy, and this increases the mortality ofpatients with malignancy who receive erythropoietin. The other major risk factor associated with these drugs is ischaemic stroke.
Diabetic nephropathy is not a contraindication, and indeed patients with diabetic nephropathy often tend to be relativelyerythropoietin resistant.
Receiving haemodialysis or having had a renal transplant are not contraindications, and having beta-thalassaemia is irrelevant.

A 74-year-old man is referred to hospital from his GP.
He had been treated for essential hypertension, with bendroﬂumethiazide 2.5 mg and amiloride 10 mg daily. However, a routine check of hisrenal function revealed:
Serum sodium134 mmol/L(137-144)
Serum potassium5.9 mmol/L(3.5-4.9)
Serum urea7.0 mmol/L(2.5-7.5)
Serum creatinine100 µmol/L(60-110)
When seen in the outpatient clinic, his blood pressure is 134/86 mmHg. A 12 lead electrocardiogram is normal. The GP's letter says that theamiloride was stopped the previous day.
Which of these is the most appropriate action?
options: Give 50% dextrose with twelve units of Actrapid insulin intravenously
Give 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate intravenously
Repeat serum urea and electrolytes (U&E) in one week
explanation:
Bendroﬂumethiazide, a thiazide diuretic, inhibits sodium and chloride reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, resulting inincreased sodium and free water clearance. A secondary effect is the loss of potassium by increased secretion in the distal tubule inresponse to the increased intraluminal sodium. Therefore, bendroﬂumethiazide may cause hypokalaemia.
Amiloride, a potassium sparing diuretic is occasionally prescribed with thiazide or loop diuretics, to prevent hypokalaemia. It inhibitsthe movement of sodium through channels towards the end of the distal tubule and collecting ducts, preventing the passage ofsodium from the urinary space into the tubular cells. This action causes hyperpolarisation of the apical plasma membrane,preventing the secretion of potassium into the collecting ducts.
Hyperkalaemia is common (more than 5%), and is unaffected by concurrent potassium depleting diuretics.

explanation:

A 25-year-old man attends the renal outpatient clinic for the ﬁrst time.
His father has been diagnosed with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Following further genetic testing, the patientalso has the gene responsible for the disease.
As you counsel him about his disease, which of the following statements is most correct?
options: Flying is prohibited for this man
Approximately half of patients require dialysis by the age of 60
Routine testing for HIV is required
His children have a one in four chance of getting the disease
Yearly MRI brain scans are required to check for the possibility of cerebral aneurysms
explanation:
Approximately half of patients with ADPKD will reach end stage renal failure by the age of 60 and require renal replacement therapy.
ADPKD is an important hereditary renal condition. In this question the candidate's knowledge is tested about the disease includingappropriate counselling measures.
There is no speciﬁc prohibition on ﬂying.
There is no indication from the question stem that HIV testing is necessary.
Although patients with ADPKD can have associated cerebral aneurysms, the decision to undergo MRI scanning is usually on the basisof personal symptoms or family history of haemorrhagic stroke. There is certainly no need to have yearly MRI brain scanning at thisstage.
As an autosomal dominant condition, his children have a 50% chance of inheriting the condition.

A patient with stage 5 chronic kidney disease (CKD) attends the outpatient clinic to discuss the possibility of a renal transplant.
Which of the following is not a well-recognised side effect of ciclosporin?
explanation:
The immunosuppressant drugs used in transplant recipients can have many unwanted side effects.
Patient compliance with their immunosuppressants is vital for the survival of the graft, hence patients need to be well informed ofthe likely effects of these drugs as part of the pre-transplant counselling process.
Ciclosporin is not typically associated with the development of Dupuytren's contracture.
It is noteworthy that ciclosporin toxicity is itself a cause of renal failure, and is a common cause of end stage renal failure inrecipients of other transplanted organs (pancreas, liver, etc).
Ciclosporin may also be associated with chronic failure of a transplanted kidney.

explanation:
Dairy products are  high in phosphate content. Of the foods listed, cheddar cheese will contain the highest phosphate.
Phosphate level is important to control in patients with chronic renal failure.
Although high phosphate can cause symptoms such as itching, there are long term adverse cardiovascular effects.
Foods that are characteristically rich in phosphate include dairy products, ﬁbre rich foods, chocolate, and processed meats.
All of the other options have lower phosphate content than cheddar cheese and so should not be selected.

A 22-year-old female with a six week history of Henoch-Schönlein purpura is reviewed in outpatients.
On examination her blood pressure is measured at 158/90 mmHg. There is a non-blanching maculopapular rash over the back, buttocks andlower legs. She is otherwise well.
Investigations reveal:
Serum urea8 mmol/L(2.5-7.5)
Serum creatinine118 µmol/L(60-110)
Serum albumin30 g/L (37-49)
Urinalysis Protein 0
blood +
What would be the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
This lady has a diagnosis of Henoch-Schönlein purpura with minimal renal involvement (mild haematuria only).
It can present one to three days following an infection affecting an IgA-secreting mucous membrane (commonly followingpharyngitis, but can occur following infection of the gastrointestinal tract, bladder or breast).
The main presentation is with painless macroscopic haematuria, but in others it can be microscopic haematuria and proteinuria, andless commonly nephrotic syndrome.
The rash is due to a cutaneous vasculitis, and the abdominal pain is due to gut vasculitis, which may be severe in some cases, leadingto bloody diarrhoea. Arthralgia is a common symptom.

A 78-year-old Caucasian woman with known chronic kidney disease wants to know what factors are likely to affect the progression of herrenal impairment. 
Which of the following modiﬁable risk factors is most likely to be signiﬁcant in the progression of her renal impairment?
options: Short term non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drug use
explanation:
Hypertension, diabetes and the presence of proteinuria are well-recognised and accepted risk factors for the progression of chronickidney disease (CKD). 
Cardiovascular disease is also a known risk factor for progression in chronic renal impairment. 
In patients with chronic kidney disease these risk factors should be actively managed to slow any fall in glomerular ﬁltration rate.
Aspirin usage has been suggested as a possible risk factor for the progression of chronic kidney disease. However it is widely used inpatients with cardiovascular disease, which in itself is a risk factor for progression of chronic kidney disease. This is a signiﬁcantconfounding factor in the evidence base investigating a link between the drug and progressive decline in glomerular ﬁltration rate. 
The evidence that smoking and ethnicity (Afro-Caribbean and Asian ethnicity) are risk factors for CKD progression is suggestive butinconclusive. 
There is no signiﬁcant evidence that obesity affects the progression in CKD. 
Short term non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drug use is associated with a reversible decline in glomerular ﬁltration rate.  Chronic usein patients with CKD may be associated with a progressive and irreversible fall in glomerular ﬁltration rate. 
The other factor considered a risk factor for CKD progression is urinary tract outﬂow obstruction.

She undergoes a renalbiopsy and is diagnosised as having minimal change nephropathy. She initially goes into remission with oral prednisolone but on withdrawalof steroids relapses quickly.
She is readmitted with a painful left leg and further signiﬁcant oedema. D-dimers are elevated and a deep vein thrombosis extending to herexternal iliac vein is diagnosised on Doppler ultrasonography. She is commenced on heparin but symptoms fail to respond. She is back onoral prednisolone and diurectics. Her albumin remains at 20.
On examination she has gross oedema of both legs and some mild facial swelling. Her Left leg is painful and erythematous with a dusky hue.JVP is not raised. Her BP lying is 110/70 mmHg and standing is 102/62 mmHg.

APTT ratio1.86

explanation:
ATIII deﬁciency is likely as nephrotics often lose antithrombin in the urine.
Hodgkin's disease can cause minimal change disease but there is nothing in the history to suggest this.
She has no postural drop so dehydration is unlikely in the presence of oedema.
Anti-phospholipid syndrome does not cause minimal change nephropathy.

A 63-year-old man is referred by his GP to the renal outpatient clinic.
He was recently started on an ACE inhibitor for poorly-controlled hypertension, but on checking his urea and electrolytes one week later theGP was alarmed to ﬁnd a marked deterioration in his renal function. An MR angiogram demonstrated a patent right renal artery and stenosisof the left renal artery.
On examination the BP is 149/90 mmHg, urinalysis negative, normal physical examination.
Which of the following is most appropriate?
options: Refer for renal artery angioplasty +/- stenting
explanation:
This man has unilateral renal artery stenosis (RAS), and this is the most likely cause for his hypertension. The current evidencefavours medical therapy in these patients, that is, an antiplatelet agent (aspirin), lipid lowering therapy (simvastatin) and tight bloodpressure control (amlodipine).
This man is most likely to come to harm through uncontrolled hypertension and so it is most important to control his bloodpressure, but with an alternative to ACE inhibition in the ﬁrst instance. Cautious, low dose ACE inhibition is sometimes an option inthese patients when other agents have failed to reduce the blood pressure, but this should only occur under close supervision.
RAS is often unmasked when patients commence an ACE inhibitor, as these drugs reduce vasoconstriction in the efferent arterioles,which in turn reduces glomerular ﬁltration pressure. In patients with critical RAS this can often prompt a precipitous drop inglomerular ﬁltration rate.
The recently reported ASTRAL trial was a randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing medical and interventional (renal arteryangioplasty and stenting) approaches to treating RAS. It found that revascularisation carried signiﬁcant risks and conferred nosigniﬁcant clinical beneﬁt. There is some controversy over the trial recruitment strategy as it only included patients with establishedRAS where the responsible clinician was "unsure if revascularisation would be beneﬁcial", but for now current practice is to avoidroutine referral for intervention in newly diagnosed RAS.

Usually the MPO antibody is associated with microscopic polyangiitis, whereas the PR3 antibody is associated with Granulomatosiswith polyangiitis, which is closely linked.

A 25-year-old man developed bilateral loin pain and frank haematuria.
His symptoms had started 24 hours after developing a sore throat. His blood pressure was 138/88 mmHg.
Urinalysis was positive for blood (4+) and protein (2+).
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The patient has macroscopic haematuria, proteinuria and loin pain in association with pharyngitis.
IgA nephropathy typically presents as recurrent haematuria in young men, often precipitated by upper respiratory tract infections;loin pain is well described and patients may be normotensive or hypertensive.
Although acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN) is a recognised complication of streptococcal pharyngitis, there isalways a latent period of one to two weeks between the streptococcal infection and onset of signs and symptoms of acuteglomerulonephritis (oedema, haematuria, and hypertension); loin pain is not well-recognised.
Nephrolithiasis is associated with loin pain and haematuria, but the degree of proteinuria is too great in this case.
Further Reading:

A 20-year-old student attends a barbecue with some friends to celebrate the end of term.
The next day she attends the Emergency department feeling unwell. In particular she feels breathless, nauseated, and has profuse diarrhoea.She drank some alcohol at the barbecue, and reports taking 1 g paracetamol prior to attending the emergency department with no realeffect.
Bloods show:
Hb 81 g/L (115-165)

Creatinine427 μ mol/L(60-110)

Blood ﬁlm shows fragmented cells.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This student has haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) most likely secondary to Escherichia coli 0157.
Typically this presents as a diarrhoeal illness having eaten undercooked meat, with a haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia andacute kidney injury.
Often the haematological and renal indices will worsen as the diarrhoea begins to settle.

A 79-year-old man was admitted through medical receiving two days ago with urinary retention. He had experienced urinary hesitancy for anumber of months, culminating in a few days of almost complete inability to pass urine.
A urinary catheter is inserted and he is found to have a residual urine volume of 1200 mls. A renal tract ultrasound scan demonstrates anenlarged prostate, conﬁrmed on PR examination. He is now passing 3500 ml of clear urine daily.
His medical history is unremarkable and he is on no regular medication. He tells you he is managing to drink around 2000 mls of water daily.
Which of the following would be the best course of action?
options: Fluid restrict patient to 1500 ml daily
Supplement oral intake with intravenous ﬂuids
explanation:
This man has obstructive uropathy secondary to an enlarged prostate that has now been relieved with a urinary catheter.
He is now producing a large volume of dilute urine, and over the next few days as his tubules recover their function his urine willbegin to concentrate appropriately.
The main approach to management in such patients is to ensure they remain adequately hydrated while their kidneys recover theirability to concentrate urine and manage ﬂuid balance.
The patient should not be ﬂuid restricted as this would lead to severe dehydration.
This is not a psychiatric illness hence psychiatric review is unnecessary.
Desmopressin is used in (cranial) diabetes insipidus and is not indicated in this context.

A 25-year-old lady with known SLE presents with the nephrotic syndrome.
A renal biopsy is performed and this conﬁrms diffuse proliferative glomeronephritis (WHO Class IV).
Which of the following treatment regimes would you advise?
explanation:
Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (GN) (WHO class IV) is the commonest GN in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
It also carries the worst prognosis for progression to renal failure.
Large trials have conﬁrmed the eﬃcacy of cyclophosphamide.
The usual regime would include high dose steroids and pulses of intravenous cyclophosphamide, initially given monthly for sixmonths and then quarterly.
Pulsed intravenous cyclophosphamide appears to be as effective as oral cyclophosphamide but has lower toxicity.

A GP phones the renal registrar asking for advice regarding a patient.
He has a 66-year-old man with renal disease due to type 1 diabetes mellitus. The patient is currently on enalapril, aspirin, simvastatin andinsulin. He is complaining of pain in his right big toe and the GP is convinced that it is gout but unsure as to what to prescribe. He is otherwisewell with normal vital signs.
Routine renal function tests carried out last week are shown below and have been stable for the past six months.
Laboratoryvalue Value Normal Range
Serum creatinine200 µmol/litre60-110
Which of the following medications should be advised?
explanation:
Given the patient's renal impairment and suggested diagnosis of acute gout, a trial of colchicine is the best option.
Colchicine is safe to use in renal impairment. It is generally advised to be taken to the point of onset of diarrheal symptoms, when itsuse should be discontinued. So long as the patient is adherent with the advise, renal function should not deteriorate
The ﬁrst line treatment for acute gout is a non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drug (NSAID) or colchicine. Given this patient's renalimpairment, a NSAID would be contraindicated.
Paracetamol will offer some mild pain relief but will not treat gout and so is not appropriate.
Allopurinol should not be started in an acute attack of gout.
Prednisolone is a reasonable choice but is usually tried as a second line treatment after NSAID use or colchicine.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has become acutely hypocalcaemic having had a thyroidectomy.
The surgeon has likely removed the parathyroid glands in addition to the thyroid, hence deﬁciency of parathyroid hormone andhypocalcaemia.
The parathyroids are notoriously diﬃcult to identify in the operating theatre and their removal is a recognised complication ofthyroidectomy.

Patients who have been immunosuppressed for a number of years have an increasing risk of malignancy, and are particularly at riskof developing skin cancers.

A 24-year-old man is noted to have ++++ proteinuria at the diabetic clinic, and complains of bilateral leg swelling that started one week agoafter a trivial upper respiratory infection.
He has had insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus for ﬁve years but has no clinical evidence of neuropathy, and his eye screening shows nobackground retinopathy. His random glucose in the clinic is 5.9.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Young patients who present with a nephrotic syndrome are likely to have minimal change disease, and this is usually steroidresponsive. Minimal change disease is often preceded by a trivial upper respiratory infection.
Diabetic nephropathy is less likely given the absence of other microvascular disease, and this is unlikely to present acutely as anephrotic syndrome.
IgA nephropathy is also less likely to present as an acute nephrotic syndrome, though it would certainly be included on thedifferential diagnosis of asymptomatic proteinuria in an apparently ﬁt young man. Haematuria is also likely to be present.
There are no features in the history of a urinary tract infection.
Acute tubulo-interstitial nephritis would not normally cause an acute nephrotic syndrome, and (for examination purposes) thehistory would typically include a rash, a recent new medication and/or eosinophilia in the context of an acute kidney injury.

explanation:

Aspirin is indicated and should be given to this man, but this is for prognostic beneﬁt and does not address the most pressing issueof acute pulmonary oedema.

Of note, she is under surveillance for chronic renal failure (CKD stage 2), with her last creatinine measured at 120 µmol/L (60-110) threemonths before by her GP. She is on ramipril 2.5 mg once a day, alendronate 70 mg once a week, Calcichew two tablets once a day and aspirin75 mg once a day.
Her fracture is reduced with a local haematoma block and she is sent home with a week's supply of diclofenac 50 mg TDS and codeinephosphate 30 mg QDS.
She presents to her GP ﬁve days later complaining of feeling generally unwell, nauseated, and not passing as much urine. Her pulse is 85 andblood pressure is 120/70 mmHg (with no postural drop). She is not in urinary retention on clinical examination.

Creatinine350 µmol/L (60-110)

explanation: In this scenario, the recent prescription of NSAIDs after the patient's hospital attendance is the likely cause of the renal decline.NSAIDs reduce glomerular perfusion by inhibiting production of prostaglandins which dilate the afferent arteriole of the glomerulus.The reduction in blood supply to the kidney results in impairment of kidney function.

A 58-year-old man has been admitted to the medical receiving unit with a GI bleed. His past medical history includes a renal transplant that isfunctioning normally.
The patient is haemodynamically stable, but the haemoglobin is telephoned to the ward as 67 g/L. His clotting screen is within normal limits.
You decide to give a blood transfusion. The transfusion laboratory asks if there are any special requirements for the blood transfusion.
Which of these would you ask for?
explanation:
This patient is haemodynamically stable and therefore can wait for fully cross-matched irradiated units, rather than the more readilyavailable O negative or type-speciﬁc blood.
Leukocyte depleted blood is already the standard of care in the UK.
In renal transplant there is an increased risk of graft versus host disease, hence irradiated blood is indicated.

A 22-year-old female was admitted to hospital three days after a sore throat. The patient complained of abdominal pain, loose stools, wristand ankle pain.
On examination, there was a non-blanching macular-papular rash over the back, buttocks and lower legs. Her blood pressure was 175/90mmHg.
Investigations showed:

Serum albumin30 g/L (37-49)
Urinalysis Protein ++
Blood +
What would be the most appropriate ﬁrst treatment?
explanation:
This lady probably has Henoch-Schönlein nephritis (similar to IgA nephritis).
It should be diagnosed on renal biopsy. It can present one to three days following infection of an IgA secreting mucous membrane(commonly following pharyngitis, but can occur following infection of the gastrointestinal tract, bladder or breast).
The main presentation is with painless macroscopic haematuria, but in others it can be microscopic haematuria and proteinuria, andless commonly nephrotic syndrome.

A 16-year-old female patient is referred from her GP with a four day history of ankle and facial swelling and dark urine. Her last presentationat the practice was two weeks previously with pharyngitis. Blood pressure is 165/100 mmHg, and urine dipstick is strongly positive forprotein and blood.
On admission she is in acute kidney injury with a creatinine of 189 μ mumol/l and urea 17.8 mmol/l. A renal ultrasound scan shows normalsized kidneys and no sign of obstruction. After bringing her blood pressure under control, she has a renal biopsy.
Which histological features would you expect on light microscopy?
explanation:
The patient has nephritic syndrome, and the most likely cause of this is post-infectious glomerulonephritis. Wire-loop lesions may beseen in this condition. A wire-loop lesion is a capillary loop with immune complex deposition circumferential around the loop. Theymay also be seen in lupus nephritis.
Nephritic syndrome consists of:OliguriaAcute renal failureHaematuriaHypertensionProteinuriaOedema
Outcome and treatment of nephritic syndrome depends on renal biopsy.
Post-infectious glomerulonephritis is a diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with proliferation of capillaries, obliteration ofcapillary loops and 'wire-loop' lesions on light microscopy. There is antibody and compliment deposition on immunostaining.
Crescentic glomerulonephritis occurs in IgA nephropathy, small vessel vasculitis, Goodpasture's disease and systemic lupuserythematosus (SLE). It is less common in post-infectious glomerulonephritis.

A 67-year-old lady with hypertension and chronic kidney disease presents for annual review in nephrology clinic. 
Her most recent urine test reveals that the albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) is 83 mg/mmol. Her blood tests show:

(eGFR 49 ml/min/1.73 m).
What is the most appropriate target range for her blood pressure?
explanation:
The NICE guidelines on the management of Chronic kidney disease (CG182) recommend that patients with chronic kidney diseasewho have proteinuria equivalent to ACR ≥ 70 mg/mmol should have their blood pressure controlled to the target range 120-129/<80 mmHg. The same target range should be used in patients with diabetes.
The NICE guidelines recommend that a blood pressure target range of 120-139/<90 mmHg should be used in non-diabetic patientswith chronic kidney disease and an ACR <70 mg/mmol.
Aiming for lower systolic (<120 mmHg) or diastolic (<60 mmHg) blood pressures increases the risk of mortality, cardiovasculardisease, congestive cardiac failure and, in the case of low diastolic values, progression of chronic kidney disease.

explanation:
